scenes.verse: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
scenes.after: John begins before Bethlehem, before creation itself: “The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us” (John 1:14). The story that follows happens on this map.

scenes.title: Galilee to Judea, on foot.
scenes.text: Most of the story unfolds between the Sea of Galilee and Jerusalem, about 110–125 km apart in a straight line.

scenes.title: Every mark says how sure we are.
Your prayer has been heard.
scenes.text: In the time of Herod king of Judea, the priest Zechariah is chosen by lot to burn incense in the temple. An angel tells him that his wife Elizabeth, old and childless, will bear a son, John, who will go before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah. Because he does not believe, he cannot speak until the child is named.
scenes.note: The king is Herod the Great, who died about 4 BC. The angel is Gabriel (Luke 1:19), who comes to Mary in Elizabeth’s sixth month (Luke 1:26, 36). Zechariah and Elizabeth lived in “a town in the hill country of Judah” (Luke 1:39), which Luke does not name.
scenes.life: Priests served in 24 divisions, each taking its turn on duty in the temple (1 Chronicles 24); Abijah was the eighth (1 Chronicles 24:10). There were so many priests that the honor of burning incense was given by lot (Luke 1:9).

scenes.title: Do not be afraid, Mary.
scenes.text: In Nazareth, a small town in Galilee, the angel Gabriel tells Mary, a virgin pledged to marry Joseph, that she will bear a son and name Him Jesus. “I am the Lord’s servant,” she answers.
scenes.note: Matthew tells the news from Joseph’s side: in a dream an angel tells him to take Mary as his wife (Matthew 1:18–25). Nazareth was a farming village of probably a few hundred people.
scenes.life: A betrothal was legally binding: Matthew says Joseph planned to end it quietly, which needed a divorce (Matthew 1:19). The couple usually lived apart for a time, often about a year, before the wedding.
scenes.found: In 2009 archaeologists uncovered remains of a house from Jesus’ time in Nazareth, near the Church of the Annunciation: a rare look at the small village.

scenes.title: Mary visits Elizabeth.
scenes.text: Mary hurries to the hill country to see her relative Elizabeth, who is expecting John. Elizabeth blesses her, and Mary praises God. Months later John is born, and his father Zechariah prophesies.
scenes.note: Luke names only “a town in the hill country of Judah”. Ein Karem, west of Jerusalem, marks a later tradition.
scenes.life: A child was named at his circumcision on the eighth day, with relatives and neighbors present (Luke 1:59). Zechariah, unable to speak, writes the name on a tablet: “His name is John.”

scenes.title: A census of the whole empire.
scenes.text: Caesar Augustus orders a registration, and everyone goes to his own town to be registered. The decree comes from Rome, far to the west.
scenes.note: Luke ties this to a census taken while Quirinius governed Syria. How to date that census against other records is still debated. The red shows Rome’s empire around the time of Jesus’ birth: deep red for provinces Rome governed, light red for kingdoms ruled for Rome by allied kings, such as Herod’s. The borders are approximate.

scenes.title: To the city of David.
scenes.text: Joseph belongs to the house and line of David, so he goes up from Nazareth to Bethlehem, David’s hometown, with Mary, who is expecting a child.
scenes.note: About 110 km (70 miles) in a straight line. Luke gives no road and no travel time, so the line is schematic. Matthew later links Bethlehem with Micah’s promise of a ruler (Matthew 2:5–6; Micah 5:2).

scenes.title: Laid in a manger.
scenes.text: While they are there, Mary gives birth to her firstborn son. She wraps Him in cloths and lays Him in a manger, because there is no room for them in the lodging.
scenes.note: Luke’s word (katalyma) can mean an inn or a guest room; he uses it again for the upper room (Luke 22:11). The Church of the Nativity marks a cave tradition recorded by the second century.
scenes.life: Village houses often had a family room raised a little above a lower area where animals were brought in at night, with mangers set in the floor or wall. A manger could be inside the home, not only in a stable.

scenes.verse: Today in the city of David a Savior has been born to you. He is Christ the Lord!
scenes.after: Shepherds keeping watch over their flocks hear the angel, go to Bethlehem, and find Mary, Joseph and the baby (Luke 2:8–20). The exact fields are unknown.

scenes.title: A light for the Gentiles.
scenes.text: Mary and Joseph bring Jesus to the temple to present Him to the Lord. Simeon calls Him a light for the Gentiles; the prophet Anna gives thanks and speaks about Him.
scenes.life: Mary and Joseph offer two birds, the offering the law allowed when a family could not afford a lamb (Luke 2:24; Leviticus 12:8).

scenes.title: Visitors from the east.
scenes.text: Magi come to Jerusalem asking for the newborn king. Sent on to Bethlehem, they find the child with Mary, worship Him and offer gold, frankincense and myrrh, then return home another way.
scenes.note: Matthew does not say how many Magi came; “three” comes from the three gifts. He places the visit in a house, and Herod’s order about boys two and under suggests it came some time after the birth (Matthew 2:16). Luke and Matthew each tell part of these years; this order is a common way of fitting them together.
scenes.life: The word magi was used of a learned priestly class in Persia and Babylon, known for interpreting dreams and the stars; Matthew says only that they came “from the east”. Frankincense and myrrh came from southern Arabia and the Horn of Africa, and both were costly.

scenes.title: Taken to safety.
scenes.text: An angel warns Joseph that Herod intends to kill the child. Joseph takes the child and His mother by night and leaves for Egypt. Herod orders the killing of the boys in and around Bethlehem.
scenes.note: Matthew names Egypt but no town and no road, so later route traditions are not drawn. No other source records the killings at Bethlehem, a small village; the historian Josephus does record Herod’s brutal last years, including the execution of three of his own sons.

scenes.title: Growing in wisdom.
scenes.text: After Herod dies, Matthew says, the family returns from Egypt and settles in Nazareth. Luke adds that the child grows and becomes strong, filled with wisdom, and the grace of God is upon Him (Luke 2:39–40).
scenes.note: Matthew says Joseph avoided Judea because Herod’s son Archelaus ruled there, and withdrew to Galilee (Matthew 2:19–23). Rome removed Archelaus in AD 6. The Gospels leave most of these years unrecorded.
scenes.life: Joseph was a tektōn, a builder who worked in wood and stone, and Mark calls Jesus one too (Matthew 13:55; Mark 6:3). Sepphoris, the city Herod Antipas rebuilt as his capital, lay about 6 km from Nazareth.

scenes.title: At twelve, in the temple.
scenes.text: After the Passover, the boy Jesus stays behind. His parents find Him three days later in the temple courts, listening to the teachers and asking them questions.
scenes.life: Families went up to Jerusalem for Passover in large groups of relatives and friends, which is how a boy could be missed for a day (Luke 2:44).

scenes.title: The fifteenth year of Tiberius.
scenes.text: Luke dates John’s preaching by the rulers of the day, usually placed around AD 28–29. Jesus was about thirty (Luke 3:23).

scenes.title: Baptized by John.
scenes.text: Jesus comes from Nazareth and is baptized by John in the Jordan. The Spirit descends on Him like a dove.
scenes.note: Mark names the Jordan, not a crossing. The marked baptism site is a later tradition.
scenes.found: The Jewish historian Josephus, writing around AD 93, describes John the Baptist as a good man who urged the Jews to live righteously and to be baptized (Antiquities 18.116–119).

scenes.verse: And a voice came from heaven: “You are My beloved Son; in You I am well pleased.”

scenes.title: Forty days of testing.
scenes.text: The Spirit leads Jesus into the wilderness, where He is tempted by the devil. He answers each temptation with Scripture.
scenes.note: The Gospels do not name the place. Matthew and Luke also set one temptation at the temple in Jerusalem.

scenes.title: The first followers.
scenes.text: John the Baptist points to Jesus as the Lamb of God. Andrew follows Him and brings his brother Simon; Philip and Nathanael soon join them.
scenes.note: John names “Bethany beyond the Jordan”. Its exact location is unresolved, so the map marks a region, not a point. Philip and Nathanael are called the next day, as Jesus sets out for Galilee (John 1:43).

scenes.title: Water into wine.
scenes.text: At a wedding, the wine runs out. Jesus has servants fill six stone jars with water, and it becomes wine. John calls it the first of His signs.
scenes.note: Two sites claim Cana: Kafr Kanna, honored today, and Khirbet Qana to the north, which Byzantine and Crusader pilgrims venerated and many archaeologists now favor. The atlas shows both.
scenes.life: John says the jars were for Jewish purification (John 2:6). Stone was used because, under purity rules, it could not become unclean. A village wedding could last several days, and running out of wine would have embarrassed the hosts.
scenes.found: Workshops that carved stone vessels in the early Roman period have been excavated in Galilee, including one at Reina, beside Kafr Kanna. They show how common purity jars like Cana’s were.

scenes.title: My Father’s house.
scenes.text: At Passover, Jesus drives the traders and money changers out of the temple courts and tells them not to make His Father’s house a marketplace.
scenes.note: John places a temple cleansing at the start of the ministry; the other Gospels place one in the last week.

scenes.title: You must be born again.
scenes.text: Nicodemus, a teacher of Israel, comes to Jesus at night. Jesus tells him that no one can see the kingdom of God unless he is born again, and no one can enter it unless he is born of water and the Spirit.
scenes.note: John does not name the house. The circle marks the city, not a building.
scenes.life: Nicodemus was a Pharisee and “a leader of the Jews” (John 3:1). John mentions him twice more: defending Jesus before the council (John 7:50–51) and bringing spices for His burial (John 19:39).

scenes.verse: For God so loved the world that He gave His one and only Son, that everyone who believes in Him shall not perish but have eternal life.

scenes.title: Living water.
scenes.text: On His way from Judea to Galilee, Jesus rests at Jacob’s well about the sixth hour and asks a Samaritan woman for a drink. Many in her town come to believe.
scenes.note: When the woman speaks of worship “on this mountain” (John 4:20), she almost certainly means Mount Gerizim, the Samaritans’ holy mountain, which rises above the well.
scenes.life: Jews and Samaritans shared the Law of Moses but disagreed over where God should be worshiped. The Jewish ruler John Hyrcanus had destroyed the Samaritan temple on Gerizim in the late second century BC, and the two peoples avoided each other (John 4:9).

scenes.verse: But whoever drinks the water I give him will never thirst. Indeed, the water I give him will become in him a fount of water springing up to eternal life.

scenes.title: Good news to the poor.
scenes.text: In Nazareth’s synagogue, Jesus reads from Isaiah and announces its fulfillment. His hearers drive Him out of town, but He passes through the crowd and goes on His way.
scenes.note: Luke says the town was built on a hill, and the crowd took Him to its brow (Luke 4:29). The ridge is real terrain; the exact spot is not known.
scenes.life: On the Sabbath the synagogue gathered the village to read and explain the Law and the Prophets. A visitor could be handed the scroll and invited to speak (Luke 4:16–17; Acts 13:15).
scenes.found: In 2009 a first-century synagogue was found at Magdala, on the lake. A carved stone inside shows the temple’s menorah. It is one of very few Galilean synagogues known from Jesus’ lifetime.

scenes.title: Follow Me.
scenes.text: Jesus proclaims, “The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is near. Repent and believe in the gospel!” By the sea He calls the fishermen Simon, Andrew, James and John.
scenes.note: Matthew says Jesus left Nazareth and settled in Capernaum, by the sea (Matthew 4:13).
scenes.life: Fishing on the lake was a family business: Zebedee had hired men (Mark 1:20). Fish were salted and traded around the region; Magdala, about 8 km south-west along the shore, was probably the town the Greeks called Taricheae, “salted fish”.
scenes.found: In 1986, when drought lowered the lake, two brothers found a wooden fishing boat in the mud near Ginosar, a little north of Magdala. It dates to about the first century BC or AD and is about 8 m long: the kind of boat fishermen used on the lake in Jesus’ day.

scenes.title: A day in Capernaum.
scenes.text: In the synagogue, Jesus teaches with authority and frees a man from an unclean spirit. At the house of Simon and Andrew He heals Simon’s mother-in-law. At sunset the whole town gathers at the door.
scenes.life: The Sabbath ended at sunset. Only then could people carry the sick through the streets, which is why the whole town gathers at the door after dark (Mark 1:32–33).
scenes.found: The white limestone synagogue that visitors see at Capernaum today was built centuries later, over an older basalt floor that its excavators date to the first century.

scenes.title: Get up, pick up your mat, and walk.
scenes.text: At the pool of Bethesda, by the Sheep Gate, Jesus heals a man who has been disabled for thirty-eight years. It is the Sabbath, and the controversy begins.
scenes.note: John names the pool. Excavated pools north of the temple are widely identified with it.
scenes.found: Excavations north of the temple uncovered two large pools divided by a central wall. A colonnade on each side and one across the middle would make John’s five colonnades (John 5:2).

scenes.title: Authority to forgive.
scenes.text: Friends lower a paralyzed man through the roof. Jesus forgives his sins, then tells him to get up, take his mat and go home. He does.
scenes.note: Excavated Capernaum had one-storey basalt houses around shared courtyards, roofed with beams and packed earth. The houses here are illustrative; the village’s exact extent is not known.
scenes.life: Roofs were flat, made of beams covered with branches and packed earth, and reached by an outside stair. People worked, dried produce and slept on them.
scenes.found: Excavations at Capernaum uncovered basalt houses from Jesus’ time. One, beneath a later octagonal church, was honored as Peter’s house from early on; its plastered walls carry graffiti left by Christian pilgrims.

scenes.title: Calling sinners.
scenes.text: Jesus calls Levi from his tax booth. At a meal with tax collectors and sinners, He says He came to call not the righteous, but sinners.
scenes.life: Tolls were collected by locals who bought the right and kept the surplus, so tax collectors were widely despised. Capernaum sat near the border between Herod Antipas’s Galilee and his brother Philip’s territory, and goods crossing it paid toll.

scenes.title: He begins to teach.
scenes.text: Jesus goes up on a mountainside and teaches His disciples: the Beatitudes, salt and light, love for enemies, the Lord’s Prayer, and the house built on the rock.
scenes.note: Matthew does not name the mountain. The Mount of Beatitudes marks a later tradition.

scenes.title: Compassion and faith.
scenes.text: A centurion trusts Jesus to heal his servant with a word. At the gate of Nain, Jesus raises a widow’s only son and gives him back to his mother.
scenes.life: Burial usually took place the same day as death. A widow who lost her only son also lost her support and her family’s future.

scenes.title: Teaching from a boat.
scenes.text: The crowd is so large that Jesus teaches from a boat. A sower, a growing seed, a mustard seed: ordinary things become windows on the kingdom.

scenes.kicker: The other side of the sea
scenes.title: Restored, and sent to tell.
scenes.text: On the crossing, Jesus calms a storm with a word. On the far shore He frees a man from unclean spirits and sends him home to tell what the Lord has done, and the man proclaims it in the Decapolis.
scenes.note: The crossing is recorded, but not where they landed. The eastern shore is marked as a region.

scenes.title: Do not be afraid; just believe.
scenes.text: On the way to Jairus’s house, a woman touches Jesus’ cloak and is healed. Then He takes Jairus’s daughter by the hand and raises her.
scenes.life: Families hired mourners and flute players at a death (Matthew 9:23). A later Jewish rule says even the poorest husband should provide at least two flutes and one wailing woman for his wife’s funeral.

scenes.title: The Twelve are sent.
scenes.text: Jesus sends the Twelve out two by two. They preach repentance, drive out demons and heal the sick.

scenes.kicker: Herod’s fortress · east of the Dead Sea
scenes.title: John is killed.
scenes.text: Herod Antipas has imprisoned John the Baptist for condemning his marriage to Herodias. At a birthday banquet, bound by an oath, he has John beheaded. John’s disciples bury his body.
scenes.note: Mark does not name the place. Josephus, the first-century Jewish historian, says John was held and killed at Herod’s fortress of Machaerus, and that some Jews saw Herod’s later defeat by the Nabatean king Aretas as God’s judgment for it (Antiquities 18.116–119).

scenes.kicker: A solitary place by the sea
scenes.title: Bread for the multitude.
scenes.text: Five loaves and two fish. Jesus gives thanks, and five thousand men are fed, with twelve baskets left over.
scenes.note: Luke places it near Bethsaida (Luke 9:10). The exact spot is not given.
scenes.life: John says the boy’s five loaves were barley (John 6:9), the cheaper bread most poor families ate.

scenes.kicker: On the sea · the fourth watch
scenes.title: Take courage! It is I.
scenes.text: Jesus sends the disciples ahead by boat toward Bethsaida and goes up the mountain to pray. In the night they strain at the oars against the wind. He comes to them walking on the sea, and the wind dies down.
scenes.note: Mark gives the direction of travel, not the route, so none is drawn.
scenes.life: The Romans divided the night into four watches. The fourth ran from about 3 a.m. to dawn, after a whole night of rowing against the wind.

scenes.verse: Jesus answered, “I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to Me will never hunger, and whoever believes in Me will never thirst.”

scenes.kicker: IV · Beyond Galilee · region of Tyre
scenes.title: Faith beyond the border.
scenes.text: A Gentile mother pleads for her daughter, and because of her answer Jesus heals the girl. Then He goes through Sidon to the Sea of Galilee and the Decapolis.
scenes.note: Mark 7:31 gives the order of places, not the roads.

scenes.title: Sight restored.
scenes.text: People bring a blind man to Jesus. He leads him out of the village and heals him in two stages, until he sees everything clearly.
scenes.note: Bethsaida’s site is debated between et-Tell and el-Araj.

scenes.title: Who do you say I am?
scenes.text: On the road, Jesus asks His disciples who they say He is. Peter answers that He is the Christ. Jesus then begins to speak of His suffering, death and rising.
scenes.found: At Banias, the site of Caesarea Philippi, the cave and rock-cut niches of a shrine to the god Pan can still be seen. Philip rebuilt the town and named it for Caesar.

scenes.verse: Then Jesus called the crowd to Him along with His disciples, and He told them, “If anyone wants to come after Me, he must deny himself and take up his cross and follow Me.”

scenes.title: The transfiguration.
scenes.text: Jesus takes Peter, James and John up a high mountain. He is transfigured before them, Moses and Elijah appear, and a voice says, “This is My beloved Son. Listen to Him!”
scenes.note: The Gospels do not name the mountain. An early tradition names Mount Tabor; others suggest Mount Hermon, near Caesarea Philippi. Both are marked as later identifications.

scenes.kicker: V · Toward Jerusalem · on the journey
scenes.title: Who is my neighbor?
scenes.text: Jesus sets out resolutely for Jerusalem. On the way, a lawyer asks who his neighbor is, and Jesus tells of a Samaritan who shows mercy.
scenes.note: Luke 9:51 begins the journey. Many episodes on it have no named place. The parable itself is set on the road down from Jerusalem to Jericho (Luke 10:30), the same climb Jesus later makes in the other direction.

scenes.kicker: An unnamed place · the lost son
scenes.verse: For this son of mine was dead and is alive again! He was lost and is found!’ So they began to celebrate.
scenes.after: Tax collectors and sinners draw near, and Jesus tells of a lost sheep, a lost coin and a lost son (Luke 15).

scenes.title: Ten are cleansed. One returns.
scenes.text: Ten men with leprosy call out to Jesus. All ten are healed on the way; one, a Samaritan, comes back to give thanks.
scenes.life: People with skin diseases had to live apart and warn others by crying out “Unclean, unclean!” (Leviticus 13:45–46). Only a priest could declare them clean, which is why Jesus sends them to the priests (Luke 17:14).

scenes.title: Teaching at the feast.
scenes.text: Halfway through the feast, Jesus teaches in the temple courts. On the last day He cries out, “If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink.”
scenes.life: During this feast, priests carried water each morning from the Pool of Siloam to pour out at the altar, and great lamps lit the temple courts at night (Mishnah, Sukkah 4–5). Jesus’ words about living water (John 7:37–38), and perhaps about the light of the world (John 8:12), may echo that background.

scenes.title: Sent to Siloam.
scenes.text: Jesus puts mud on the eyes of a man born blind and sends him to wash in the pool of Siloam. He comes back seeing.
scenes.note: A Second Temple–era pool excavated in 2004 at the south end of the city is widely identified with it.

scenes.title: The good shepherd.
scenes.text: Jesus calls Himself the gate for the sheep and the good shepherd, who knows His own and lays down His life for the sheep. He has other sheep too, and there will be one flock and one shepherd.
scenes.life: At night, flocks were kept in walled sheepfolds. A shepherd led his sheep out rather than driving them, and they knew his voice (John 10:3–4).

scenes.title: In Solomon’s Colonnade.
scenes.text: In winter, Jesus walks in Solomon’s Colonnade. Asked whether He is the Christ, He points to His works and says: “I and the Father are one.”
scenes.note: Solomon’s Colonnade ran along the temple courts; its exact line is reconstructed.
scenes.life: The Feast of Dedication, Hanukkah, remembers how the Maccabees cleansed and rededicated the temple in 164 BC after a Greek king had defiled it (1 Maccabees 4).

scenes.title: Back across the Jordan.
scenes.text: Jesus goes back across the Jordan to the place where John first baptized, and many there believe in Him.

scenes.title: Lazarus is raised.
scenes.text: Lazarus has died. Jesus meets Martha and Mary, and He weeps. Then He calls Lazarus out of the tomb, and he comes out.
scenes.life: The tomb was a cave with a stone across the entrance (John 11:38). Mourning customarily lasted seven days, and many came from nearby Jerusalem to console the sisters (John 11:18–19).

scenes.verse: Jesus said to her, “I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in Me will live, even though he dies.”

scenes.title: A withdrawal to Ephraim.
scenes.text: The council plans to put Jesus to death, so He no longer moves about openly. He withdraws with His disciples to a town called Ephraim.
scenes.note: Ephraim is often identified with et-Taiyibeh, north-east of Jerusalem. The identification is uncertain.

scenes.title: Receiving the kingdom like a child.
scenes.text: Crowds gather again. Jesus welcomes the little children, and a rich man walks away sad when told to give up his wealth and follow.

scenes.title: To seek and to save.
scenes.text: Passing through Jericho, Jesus calls Zacchaeus down from a sycamore tree and stays at his house. The tax collector gives half his goods to the poor.
scenes.life: Jericho was a rich oasis on the trade road, famed for its date palms and balsam, so a chief tax collector could grow wealthy. Sycamore-figs have short trunks and low, spreading branches that are easy to climb.
scenes.found: Herod’s winter palaces, with pools and gardens, have been excavated at New Testament Jericho. Herod the Great died there, usually dated 4 BC.

scenes.title: Bartimaeus follows on the way.
scenes.text: A blind beggar calls out to Jesus as He leaves Jericho. Healed, he follows Jesus along the road, the road that leads up to Jerusalem.
scenes.note: Mark places the healing as Jesus leaves Jericho; Luke, as He approaches it (Luke 18:35). From Jericho, below sea level, the way to Jerusalem climbs about 1,000 m through the wilderness. The line is schematic.

scenes.title: Holy Week.
scenes.text: From Jericho the road goes up toward Bethany and Jerusalem. Mark gives six of his sixteen chapters to these last days.
guide: Open the Holy Week guide: people, the cross, the tomb, history

scenes.title: Anointed at Bethany.
scenes.text: At a dinner, Mary anoints Jesus’ feet with costly perfume. Judas objects; Jesus connects her act with His burial.
scenes.note: Mark and Matthew tell of an anointing at Bethany in the house of Simon the Leper, on Jesus’ head (Mark 14:3–9); whether it is the same event is debated.

scenes.title: The king enters Jerusalem.
scenes.text: Jesus rides a colt down toward the city as the crowd praises God. When He sees the city, He weeps over it. No gate or road is named.
scenes.life: Tens of thousands of pilgrims, perhaps many more, crowded Jerusalem at Passover. The crowd’s words come from Psalm 118, sung at the festivals, and palm branches (John 12:13) had been a national symbol since the Maccabees.

scenes.title: A house of prayer.
scenes.text: Jesus overturns the money changers’ tables and teaches that the temple is to be a house of prayer for all nations.
scenes.life: The temple tax had to be paid in silver shekels from Tyre, prized for their purity, so money changers swapped other coins for them. Sellers provided animals that met the requirements for sacrifice.
scenes.found: Two stone notices from the temple have been found, the first in 1871. In Greek they warn foreigners not to pass the barrier into the inner courts, on pain of death. Gentiles could pray only in the outer court, which gives weight to Jesus’ words about “all the nations”.

scenes.verse: Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind and with all your strength.
scenes.after: Asked which commandment is first, Jesus joins it with love for one’s neighbor (Mark 12:28–34).

scenes.kicker: Mount of Olives · opposite the temple
scenes.title: Watch and stay faithful.
scenes.text: Sitting opposite the temple, Jesus warns Peter, James, John and Andrew of deception and coming distress, and tells them again and again to keep watch.
scenes.found: Excavations beside the Western Wall uncovered huge stones thrown down from the temple mount when the Romans destroyed the temple in AD 70, as Jesus had said would happen (Mark 13:2).

scenes.title: Bread and the cup.
scenes.text: In a furnished upper room, Jesus shares the Passover meal with the Twelve and gives them bread and the cup. In John’s account, He washes their feet.
scenes.note: John calls the day of the crucifixion “the day of Preparation for the Passover” (John 19:14; compare 18:28), and how his timing fits the other Gospels is debated. The Cenacle marks a later tradition; the present building is medieval.
scenes.life: At festive meals guests reclined on couches around a low table, leaning on the left elbow. That is how the disciple Jesus loved could lean back against Him (John 13:23–25).

scenes.title: Out to the Mount of Olives.
scenes.text: After a hymn they go out. John says they cross the Kidron Valley to a garden. The path is drawn, not mapped.
scenes.life: Gethsemane means “oil press”. Olive groves covered the Mount of Olives, across the Kidron Valley from the temple.

scenes.verse: “Abba, Father,” He said, “all things are possible for You. Take this cup from Me. Yet not what I will, but what You will.”

scenes.title: Judas arrives.
scenes.text: Judas comes with an armed crowd. Jesus is arrested, and the disciples flee. John adds lanterns and torches (John 18:3) and names Peter as the swordsman and Malchus as the servant (John 18:10).

scenes.title: Before the authorities.
scenes.text: The high priest’s house is unlocated. Pilate’s praetorium is argued for both Herod the Great’s palace and the Antonia, so the atlas marks both and picks neither.
scenes.life: John says the council could not put anyone to death (John 18:31); Rome normally kept capital cases for its governor, though scholars debate the exceptions. Pilate normally lived at Caesarea on the coast and came up to Jerusalem with troops at festival time, when crowds and tension were greatest.
scenes.found: In 1961 a stone at Caesarea was found inscribed with the name of Pontius Pilate, prefect of Judea. In 1990 a decorated burial box inscribed “Joseph son of Caiaphas” was found in Jerusalem, and many scholars think it belonged to the high priest.

scenes.kicker: Day of Preparation · the third hour (Mark)
scenes.title: The Place of the Skull.
scenes.text: Jesus is led out to Golgotha. Mark names Simon of Cyrene carrying the cross; John says Jesus went out carrying it. The Via Dolorosa is a later devotional route and is not drawn.
scenes.note: John places Pilate’s verdict about the sixth hour (John 19:14); how the two times fit is debated.
scenes.life: Crucifixion was Rome’s punishment for slaves and rebels, carried out in public as a warning. The charge was posted above the cross, here in Hebrew, Latin and Greek (John 19:20). Hours were counted from sunrise: the third hour is about 9 a.m., the sixth about noon and the ninth about 3 p.m.
scenes.found: The Roman historian Tacitus, writing around AD 116, records that Christ suffered the death penalty under Pontius Pilate in the reign of Tiberius (Annals 15.44). Josephus also mentions Jesus, and the death of His brother James.

scenes.title: Seven sayings from the cross.
scenes.text: One of the two criminals crucified with Him asks to be remembered (Luke 23:42). Christian tradition gathers seven sayings from the four Gospels; no single Gospel has all of them.
scenes.note: The words “Father, forgive them…” (Luke 23:34) are missing from some early manuscripts.
items: Today you will be with Me in Paradise
My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?
Father, into Your hands I commit My Spirit

scenes.verse: When Jesus had received the sour wine, He said, “It is finished.” And bowing His head, He yielded up His spirit.
scenes.after: Darkness covers the land from the sixth hour to the ninth (Mark 15:33).

scenes.title: Truly this man was the Son of God!
scenes.text: Jesus breathes His last, and the curtain of the temple is torn in two from top to bottom. The centurion facing the cross says, “Truly this man was the Son of God!” Women watch from a distance.
scenes.note: Mark names Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joses, and Salome. The curtain hung in the sanctuary, shown here in the model.

scenes.title: Laid in a tomb.
scenes.text: Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus lay Jesus’ body in a new tomb in a garden near the place of crucifixion.
scenes.note: The Holy Sepulchre marks a site honored by the fourth century; most archaeologists place it outside the city walls of Jesus’ day, in an old quarry with first-century tombs. The Garden Tomb was proposed in the nineteenth century, and most archaeologists date that tomb centuries earlier, which does not fit the Gospels’ “new tomb”.
scenes.life: The body was wrapped in linen with spices (John 19:40) and laid on a bench in a rock-cut tomb. The burial had to be finished before the Sabbath began at sunset.
scenes.found: In 1968 the heel bone of a crucified man, still pierced by an iron nail, was found in a Jerusalem family tomb. It shows that the Romans nailed victims to crosses in this period, and that a crucified man could receive a proper burial.

scenes.title: Sealed and guarded.
scenes.text: The chief priests and Pharisees ask Pilate to secure the tomb until the third day. They seal the stone and post a guard.
scenes.note: Matthew adds that after the resurrection the soldiers were paid to say the disciples had stolen the body, and that the story was still told in his day (Matthew 28:11–15).
scenes.life: A seal on the stone, probably cord fixed with clay or wax, would show whether anyone had moved it.

scenes.kicker: VII · First day of the week · early
scenes.title: He is not here; He has risen!
scenes.text: Women come to the tomb at dawn with spices and find the stone rolled away. Two men in radiant apparel tell them He has risen.
scenes.life: The women came after the Sabbath to anoint the body (Mark 16:1). In that culture a woman’s testimony carried less legal weight (Josephus, Antiquities 4.219), yet all four Gospels name women as the first to find the tomb empty.

scenes.verse: Jesus said to her, “Mary.” She turned and said to Him in Hebrew, “Rabboni!” (which means “Teacher”).

scenes.kicker: The road to Emmaus · toward evening
scenes.title: Known in the breaking of bread.
scenes.text: Two followers walk to Emmaus, about seven miles from Jerusalem. A stranger explains the Scriptures; at supper He breaks the bread, and they recognize Jesus.
scenes.note: Several sites have been proposed for Emmaus. None is certain, so no place or route is drawn.

scenes.title: Peace be with you.
scenes.text: The disciples are behind locked doors. Jesus stands among them, shows them His hands and side, and sends them as the Father sent Him.
scenes.note: John does not name the house. The circle marks the city, not a building.

scenes.title: Thomas sees and believes.
scenes.text: Thomas is with them now. Jesus invites him to see and touch. Thomas answers, “My Lord and my God!”

scenes.title: Breakfast by the sea.
scenes.text: After a night of catching nothing, seven disciples cast the net where Jesus tells them. On shore He has a charcoal fire with fish and bread, and invites them to eat.
scenes.note: John names the lake, not the beach. The shoreline is marked as a region.
scenes.life: Fishermen on the lake often worked through the night (compare Luke 5:5). A charcoal fire appears only twice in the Gospels: here, and in the courtyard where Peter denied Jesus (John 18:18).

scenes.title: Feed My sheep.
scenes.text: Three times Jesus asks Peter, “Do you love Me?” Three times He gives him a charge: feed and care for My sheep. Then: “Follow Me.”

scenes.verse: …and teaching them to obey all that I have commanded you. And surely I am with you always, even to the end of the age.”
scenes.after: The eleven go to the mountain Jesus had designated, and He sends them to make disciples of all nations (Matthew 28:16–20).

scenes.kicker: VIII · Mount of Olives · toward Bethany
scenes.title: Taken up while blessing them.
scenes.text: Jesus leads His followers out as far as Bethany, lifts up His hands and blesses them, and is carried up into heaven. They return to Jerusalem with great joy.
scenes.note: Acts says they returned from the Mount of Olives (Acts 1:12). Forty days of appearances lie between Easter and this day (Acts 1:3).

scenes.title: The Spirit is poured out.
scenes.text: On the day of Pentecost, the disciples are all together in one place. A sound like a mighty rushing wind fills the house, tongues like flames of fire rest on each of them, and they speak in other tongues. Peter preaches to the crowd, and about three thousand are baptized.
scenes.note: Acts speaks of “the whole house where they were sitting” (Acts 2:2) but does not say where it stood, or where the crowd gathered. God-fearing Jews from every nation under heaven were staying in Jerusalem (Acts 2:5), and the crowd included converts to Judaism (Acts 2:10–11).
scenes.life: Pentecost, Greek for “fiftieth”, was the Feast of Weeks, fifty days counted from the day the first sheaf of the harvest was waved (Leviticus 23:15–16). It came with the firstfruits of the wheat harvest (Exodus 34:22), one of three yearly feasts at which all Israelite men were to appear before the Lord (Exodus 34:23).

scenes.title: You will be My witnesses.
scenes.verse: “But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, and you will be My witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth.”

readingPlan.title: Who do you say I am?

word: Each Gospel begins differently: Matthew with a genealogy, Mark with John the Baptist, Luke with Zechariah in the temple, John before creation.
annunciation: Matthew tells instead of an angel appearing to Joseph in a dream (Matthew 1:20–21).
birth: Matthew tells the birth from Joseph’s side; only Luke mentions the manger.
rulers: Only Luke dates the start of John’s preaching by the rulers of the day.
baptism: John does not narrate the baptism; the Baptist recalls seeing the Spirit come down on Jesus.
zeal: Matthew, Mark and Luke tell of a temple clearing in the last week (see Holy Week); whether these are one event or two is debated.
synagogue: Matthew and Mark tell of a rejection in His hometown later on; it may be the same visit or another.
fishers: Luke tells of Simon, James and John leaving everything after a great catch of fish. He does not name Andrew, and whether it is the same call is debated.
firstday: Matthew tells only the healing at Peter’s house and the evening healings, with no synagogue or Sabbath.
roof: Matthew does not mention the roof.
levi: Matthew’s Gospel calls the tax collector Matthew.
sermon: Luke’s shorter sermon, on “a level place” (Luke 6:17), shares much of this teaching.
nain: Matthew tells only of the centurion’s servant; the widow of Nain is in Luke alone. John 4:46–54 tells of a royal official’s son healed from a distance; whether it is the same event is debated.
gerasenes: Matthew tells of two men, in the region of the Gadarenes.
jairus: Matthew does not name Jairus, and has the father say his daughter “has just died” (Matthew 9:18).
john: Luke does not tell of the death itself. He tells of John’s imprisonment (Luke 3:19–20) and reports Herod saying, “I beheaded John” (Luke 9:9).
loaves: The only miracle before Easter told in all four Gospels.
walking: Only Matthew tells of Peter walking on the water.
tyre: Matthew calls the woman a Canaanite.
confession: Luke does not name the place.
lost: Matthew has the lost sheep in a different setting (Matthew 18:12–14).
bartimaeus: Matthew tells of two blind men; Luke sets the healing as Jesus approached Jericho.
anoint: Matthew and Mark tell of an anointing at Bethany in the home of Simon the Leper, told just after noting the Passover was two days away, and on His head, and do not name the woman; John has six days before and His feet. Whether it is the same event is debated. Luke 7:36–50 tells of an anointing at a Pharisee’s house, usually taken as a separate event.
entry: Only Luke tells of Jesus weeping over the city (Luke 19:41–44). Matthew mentions a donkey and her colt (Matthew 21:2–7).
temple: Matthew sets it on the day of the entry; Mark, the next day. Only Mark has “for all the nations” (Mark 11:17). John tells of a temple clearing early in the ministry (John 2:13–22).
greatest: Luke does not tell this exchange here, though Luke 20:39–40 echoes its close. In Luke 10:25–28, earlier, an expert in the law asks about eternal life and gives the same two commandments.
watch: Only Mark names the four listeners; Matthew also sets it on the Mount of Olives (Matthew 24:3). Luke gives no place beyond the temple.
upper: John tells of the meal and the foot washing, but not the bread and the cup.
pray: John mentions the garden but no prayer there; compare John 12:27 and 18:11. Luke 22:43–44 is missing from some early manuscripts.
trials: Only Luke tells of the hearing before Herod Antipas; only John tells that Jesus was taken first to Annas (John 18:13–24).
sayings: No Gospel records all seven; each saying comes from one or two of them.
finished: Only John records “It is finished.” Matthew, Mark and Luke tell of the darkness and a loud cry as He died.
torn: In Luke the curtain is torn before Jesus dies, and the centurion says, “Surely this was a righteous man” (Luke 23:45–47). Only Matthew adds the earthquake and the raised saints (Matthew 27:51–53).
burial: Only John tells that Nicodemus helped (John 19:39); Matthew says the tomb was Joseph’s own (Matthew 27:60).
risen: All four name Mary Magdalene, with different companions. At the tomb Matthew tells of an angel, Mark of a young man in white, Luke of two men in radiant clothes; in John, Mary later sees two angels (John 20:12). All four agree the tomb was found empty early on the first day of the week.
mary: Matthew tells of Jesus meeting the women as they ran from the tomb (Matthew 28:9–10).
ascension: Acts, addressed to the same Theophilus, tells it again (Acts 1:1, 9–11). Some early manuscripts of Luke 24:51 lack “and was carried up into heaven.”

zechariah.note: The angel says John will go before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah, “to turn the hearts of the fathers to their children”.

birth.note: Matthew quotes it: the virgin will bear a son, and they will call Him Immanuel, “God with us”.

magi.note: The chief priests and scribes quote it to Herod: a ruler will come from Bethlehem.

egypt.note: “Out of Egypt I called My Son.” In Hosea the words refer to Israel; Matthew says Jesus’ stay in Egypt fulfilled them.
Rachel weeping for her children, recalled at the killing of Bethlehem’s boys.

nazareth.note: “He will be called a Nazarene.” Matthew cites the prophets in general; no single passage matches these words.

present.note: Mary and Joseph do what the Law requires: the firstborn is consecrated, and a pair of turtledoves or young pigeons is offered.

baptism.note: Mark opens by quoting both for John the Baptist: a messenger sent ahead, a voice calling in the wilderness.

wilderness.note: Jesus answers each temptation with Deuteronomy. The devil quotes Psalm 91:11–12.

zeal.note: The disciples remember: “Zeal for Your house will consume Me.”

nicodemus.note: As Moses lifted up the snake in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up.

synagogue.note: Jesus reads Isaiah 61:1–2, with a line from Isaiah 58:6, and says, “Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing.”

fishers.note: Matthew says Jesus’ move to Capernaum fulfilled it: “a light has dawned.”

firstday.note: Matthew quotes it at the evening healings: “He took up our infirmities.”

sermon.note: “You have heard that it was said…” Jesus quotes the Law, then goes deeper: “But I tell you.”

levi.note: Jesus answers His critics: “I desire mercy, not sacrifice.”

parables.note: Jesus quotes it to explain why He teaches in parables.
Matthew quotes it: “I will open My mouth in parables.”

bread.note: The crowd recalls the manna; Jesus answers that His Father gives the true bread from heaven, and says, “I am the bread of life.”
“And they will all be taught by God.”

samaritan.note: Asked “What is written in the Law?”, the expert in the law answers with these two commands.

booths.note: Jesus promises streams of living water, “as the Scripture has said”. No single passage matches; John explains He meant the Spirit.

dedication.note: Jesus answers the charge of blasphemy by quoting “I have said you are gods.”

children.note: Asked about divorce, Jesus goes back to creation: “the two will become one flesh.”

entry.note: Your king comes to you, gentle and riding on a donkey.
The crowd shouts: “Hosanna! Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord!” Luke has “Blessed is the King”.

temple.note: A house of prayer for all the nations, made a den of robbers.

greatest.note: Jesus joins the two commands: love God, and love your neighbor.

In the temple courts Jesus ends the parable of the tenants with it: “The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone.” After the resurrection Peter says it of Jesus, “whom God raised from the dead” (Acts 4:10–11).

upper.note: Jesus says the betrayal fulfils it: “The one who shares My bread has lifted up his heel against Me.”
“And He was numbered with the transgressors”, which Jesus says must be fulfilled in Him.

kidron.note: After they go out to the Mount of Olives, Jesus quotes it: strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered.

trials.note: Asked if He is the Christ, Jesus answers with these words: the Son of Man at the right hand of Power, coming with the clouds.

golgotha.note: The soldiers divide His garments and cast lots for His tunic.
On the way, Jesus warns the weeping women in Hosea’s words: “Fall on us!”

sayings.note: “My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?”
“Into Your hands I commit My Spirit.”
“I am thirsty”, which John says fulfilled Scripture without naming it. Psalm 22:15, and Psalm 69:21 for the sour wine, are often compared.

finished.note: “Not one of His bones will be broken.” John does not name the passage; the words are closest to Psalm 34:20 and the Passover rule in Exodus 12:46 and Numbers 9:12.
“They will look on the One they have pierced.”

risen.note: Earlier, Jesus had pointed to Jonah: “so the Son of Man will be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth.”

Paul passes on that Christ “was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures” but does not name a passage. Many readers compare Hosea 6:2, where the words are about Israel: “on the third day He will raise us up”. The sign of Jonah, above, is also compared.

emmaus.note: Jesus explains what all the Scriptures said about Himself. Luke does not list the passages; later, to the disciples, He adds the Psalms (Luke 24:44).

pentecost.note: Peter explains: this is what Joel foretold, the Spirit poured out on all people.

Peter quotes David, “nor will You let Your Holy One see decay”, and says David “spoke about the resurrection of the Christ” (Acts 2:31). Paul quotes the same line: David decayed, but the One God raised did not (Acts 13:35–37).
Peter quotes it for Jesus, raised and exalted to the right hand of God: “Sit at My right hand.”

peace.ot: “the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms”
peace.note: Jesus opens their minds to understand the Scriptures: “The Christ will suffer and rise from the dead on the third day.” Luke does not list the passages.

reflection.word: John calls Jesus the Word through whom all things were made, who “became flesh”. What changes when you read the rest of the story with that in mind?
reflection.zechariah: Zechariah and Elizabeth had prayed for a child, and the answer came when they were old. What long-standing prayer are you still carrying?
reflection.annunciation: Mary answers, “I am the Lord’s servant.” What would it take for you to say that about something you do not yet understand?
reflection.visitation: Elizabeth blesses Mary as soon as she hears her greeting. Who has encouraged you like that, and whom could you encourage?
reflection.decree: An emperor’s order moves a young couple across the country. Where have you seen large events shape small lives, including yours?
reflection.journey: Mary and Joseph travel while she is expecting, because of an emperor’s order. What journey are you on that you did not choose?
reflection.birth: There was no room, so the Savior was laid in a manger. Where might you expect to find God in ordinary or humble places?
reflection.shepherds: The news comes first to shepherds working the night shift. What does that suggest about who this good news is for?
reflection.present: Simeon had been waiting for what he was promised. What are you waiting for, and how do you wait well?
reflection.magi: The Magi travel far and return home “by another route”. What changed path might an encounter with Jesus call for in you?
reflection.egypt: Joseph acts at once on a warning in the night. When has quick obedience protected someone you love?
reflection.nazareth: The child grew strong and was filled with wisdom in a small town. What helps you grow in the quiet, unremarkable years?
reflection.twelve: His parents searched for three days. Have you ever looked for God in the wrong place, and where did you find Him?
reflection.rulers: Luke names the powerful, then says the word of God came to John in the wilderness. Where does God’s word reach you today?
reflection.baptism: Jesus begins by being baptized among ordinary people. What does it mean to you that He stood in line with them?
reflection.voice: The Father calls Jesus beloved before any miracle or teaching. How does being loved first change how you live?
reflection.wilderness: Jesus answers each temptation with Scripture. Which words of Scripture help you when you are tested?
reflection.followers: Jesus asks, “What do you want?” and then says, “Come and see.” How would you answer Him today?
reflection.cana: The servants obey before they see anything change. Where is He asking you to fill the jars and trust?
reflection.zeal: Jesus clears out what had crowded the place of prayer. What crowds out prayer in your life?
reflection.nicodemus: Nicodemus comes by night with honest questions. What question would you bring to Jesus if no one else were listening?
reflection.so-loved: God “so loved the world that He gave”. What does this verse tell you about how God sees you?
reflection.samaria: Jesus crosses lines of people, religion and custom to talk with one woman. Whom might you be avoiding?
reflection.water: Jesus offers water that ends thirst. What are you most thirsty for right now?
reflection.synagogue: His hometown could not accept that the familiar Jesus was more. Is anything too familiar for you to see freshly?
reflection.fishers: “Follow Me,” and they leave their nets at once. What nets are hard for you to put down?
reflection.firstday: Even at sunset the whole town is at His door. What need would you bring to that door tonight?
reflection.bethesda: Jesus asks a man who had waited 38 years, “Do you want to get well?” Why might that be a real question for us too?
reflection.roof: Four friends carry a man to Jesus and make a way through the roof. Who needs you to carry them to Him?
reflection.levi: Jesus eats with people others avoided. Whom would He sit down with in your town?
reflection.sermon: Of all this teaching, which line is hardest for you to live, and which do you most need to hear?
reflection.nain: Jesus sees the widow, has compassion, and says, “Do not weep.” Where do you need Him to see you?
reflection.parables: The seed is the same; the soil makes the difference. What kind of soil is your heart in this season?
reflection.gerasenes: The healed man is sent home to tell what the Lord has done. What has He done for you that you could tell?
reflection.jairus: “Do not be afraid; just believe,” after the worst news came. Where do you need to hear that today?
reflection.twelve-sent: The Twelve go out two by two with very little. What do you carry that you could do without?
reflection.john: John spoke the truth to a powerful man and paid for it. When is it costly for you to tell the truth?
reflection.loaves: A small lunch, given thanks for, feeds thousands. What small thing could you place in Jesus’ hands?
reflection.walking: “Take courage! It is I.” What storm are you rowing through right now?
reflection.bread: Jesus calls Himself the bread of life. What do you go to for nourishment, and does it satisfy?
reflection.tyre: The mother keeps asking and will not give up. What are you still praying for after a long time?
reflection.sight: The man sees in two stages. Where are you seeing only partly, and still needing His touch?
reflection.confession: “Who do you say I am?” How would you answer in your own words?
reflection.cross: Deny yourself, take up your cross, follow. What might that look like in your week?
reflection.transfig: The voice says, “Listen to Him.” What helps you listen to Jesus above other voices?
reflection.samaritan: The question turns from who my neighbor is to who acted as one. Who is your neighbor this week?
reflection.lost: The father runs to the son while he is still far off. Which son do you relate to more, and why?
reflection.ten: All ten were healed; one came back to give thanks. What could you thank God for today?
reflection.booths: “If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me.” What keeps you from coming?
reflection.siloam: The man’s story grows each time he tells it: “I was blind, but now I see.” What is your “now I see”?
reflection.shepherd: The good shepherd knows His sheep by name. How does it feel to be known that well?
reflection.dedication: Jesus points to His works when asked who He is. What has He done that helps you trust Him?
reflection.beyond: Many believed in a quiet place across the river. Where do you find room to believe away from the noise?
reflection.lazarus: Jesus weeps, though He is about to raise Lazarus. What does His grief say about yours?
reflection.resurrection-life: “Do you believe this?” Jesus asks Martha. How would you answer?
reflection.ephraim: Jesus withdraws for a time before the last journey. When do you need to step back, and with whom?
reflection.children: The kingdom belongs to those who receive it like a child. What would childlike trust look like for you?
reflection.zacchaeus: Jesus invites Himself to the house of the man everyone resented. What changed Zacchaeus: rules, or being welcomed?
reflection.bartimaeus: “What do you want Me to do for you?” What would you ask?
reflection.anoint: Mary gives something costly, and others call it waste. What would wholehearted devotion cost you?
reflection.entry: The crowd cheers, and Jesus weeps over the city. What do you think He sees that the crowd does not?
reflection.temple: A house of prayer for all the nations. Who is left out of the places where you worship?
reflection.greatest: Heart, soul, mind and strength. Which of these is hardest for you to give to God?
reflection.watch: Jesus says again and again, “Keep watch.” What helps you stay awake to what matters?
reflection.upper: “This is My body, given for you.” What does it mean to you that He gave Himself?
reflection.kidron: They sing a hymn and walk out into the night. What helps you go forward when you know a hard time is ahead?
reflection.pray: “Not what I will, but what You will.” Where are you struggling to pray that prayer?
reflection.arrest: Everyone deserted Him and fled. When have you run from what was hard, and how did He meet you afterward?
reflection.trials: The innocent one stands silent before His accusers. What strikes you most about how Jesus faced injustice?
reflection.golgotha: Simon of Cyrene is made to carry the cross for Him. Whose burden could you help carry?
reflection.sayings: Which of the words from the cross speaks most to you today, and why?
reflection.finished: “It is finished.” What in your life do you try to finish that He has already finished?
reflection.torn: A Roman soldier is the one who says, “Truly this man was the Son of God!” What led him to see it?
reflection.burial: Joseph and Nicodemus step forward when others had fled. When is it time for quiet faith to be seen?
reflection.guard: The powerful seal the stone and post a guard. What do you think can stop God’s purposes?
reflection.risen: “Why do you look for the living among the dead?” Where might you be looking for life in the wrong place?
reflection.mary: Mary knows Him when He says her name. When have you known you were known by God?
reflection.emmaus: They recognized Him in the breaking of bread. Where have you recognized Jesus in an ordinary moment?
reflection.peace: The doors are locked, yet He stands among them and says, “Peace be with you.” What fear are you locked behind?
reflection.thomas: Jesus meets Thomas’s doubt with an invitation to see and touch. What doubt would you bring to Him honestly?
reflection.breakfast: After a night of catching nothing, they find breakfast waiting. When has Jesus met you after failure?
reflection.sheep: Peter had denied Him three times; now Jesus asks him three times, “Do you love Me?” What does this tell you about how Jesus restores people?
reflection.commission: “I am with you always.” Where do you most need to remember that this week?
reflection.ascension: He leaves blessing them, and they return with great joy. How could you carry that blessing into your day?
reflection.pentecost: The Spirit came on a group of Galileans, and each listener heard them in his own language. Where do you need the Spirit’s help to speak or to listen?

people.name: Mary
people.text: A young woman of Nazareth, pledged to marry Joseph. The angel Gabriel told her that she would bear a son and name Him Jesus (Luke 1:26–38). She “treasured up all these things and pondered them in her heart” (Luke 2:19). She was at the wedding at Cana (John 2:1–5) and stood near the cross, where Jesus gave her into the care of the disciple He loved (John 19:25–27). After the ascension she was praying with the disciples (Acts 1:14).

people.name: Joseph
people.text: A descendant of David who lived in Nazareth (Luke 2:4). Matthew calls him “a righteous man” (Matthew 1:19). Guided by dreams, he took Mary as his wife, fled with the family to Egypt and brought them back to Nazareth (Matthew 1:20–24; Matthew 2:13–23). People knew Jesus as “the carpenter’s son” (Matthew 13:55). He last appears in the story when Jesus is twelve (Luke 2:41–51). During the ministry he is named only as Jesus’ father (John 6:42), and many conclude he had died by then.

people.name: Jesus’ brothers
people.text: Mark names them as James, Joses, Judas and Simon, and mentions sisters too (Mark 6:3). At first “even His own brothers did not believe in Him” (John 7:5), but after the ascension they were praying with the disciples (Acts 1:14). Paul met “James, the Lord’s brother” (Galatians 1:19) and names James among the “pillars” of the church in Jerusalem (Galatians 2:9). Many Protestants understand the brothers as later children of Mary and Joseph; Orthodox tradition sees them as Joseph’s sons from an earlier marriage, and Catholic tradition as close relatives such as cousins.

people.name: Elizabeth
people.text: Wife of the priest Zechariah, herself “a daughter of Aaron”, and a relative of Mary (Luke 1:5; Luke 1:36). Old and childless, she bore John. When Mary visited, Elizabeth, filled with the Holy Spirit, blessed her (Luke 1:41–45).

people.name: Zechariah
people.role: Priest, father of John the Baptist
people.text: A priest of the division of Abijah (Luke 1:5). While he burned incense in the temple, Gabriel told him he would have a son. Because he did not believe, he could not speak until John was born; then he praised God and prophesied (Luke 1:67–79).

people.name: John the Baptist
people.role: The prophet who prepared the way
people.text: Son of Zechariah and Elizabeth and a relative of Jesus through Mary (Luke 1:36). He preached repentance in the wilderness, baptized in the Jordan and pointed to Jesus: “Look, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:29). Herod Antipas imprisoned him and had him beheaded (Mark 6:17–29). Jesus said no one born of women was greater (Luke 7:28).

people.name: The Twelve
people.text: Jesus appointed twelve “to accompany Him, to be sent out to preach” (Mark 3:14). Mark lists Simon Peter, James and John the sons of Zebedee, Andrew, Philip, Bartholomew, Matthew, Thomas, James son of Alphaeus, Thaddaeus, Simon the Zealot and Judas Iscariot (Mark 3:16–19). Luke has Judas son of James in place of Thaddaeus (Luke 6:16); many take them to be the same man. After Judas died, Matthias took his place (Acts 1:26).

people.name: Peter
people.text: Simon, a fisherman from Bethsaida who lived in Capernaum with his brother Andrew (John 1:44; Mark 1:29). Jesus named him Cephas, which means Peter, “rock” (John 1:42). He confessed Jesus as the Christ, denied Him three times on the night of the arrest, was restored by the sea, and preached to the crowd at Pentecost (Mark 8:29; Mark 14:66–72; John 21:15–19; Acts 2:14).

people.name: Andrew
people.text: A fisherman and first a disciple of John the Baptist. He followed Jesus and brought his brother Simon to Him (John 1:40–42). At the feeding of the five thousand, he pointed out a boy with five barley loaves and two fish (John 6:8–9).

people.name: James son of Zebedee
people.text: A fisherman called with his brother John from their father’s boat (Mark 1:19–20). With Peter and John he saw the transfiguration and was near Jesus in Gethsemane (Mark 9:2; Mark 14:33). Jesus called the brothers Boanerges, “Sons of Thunder” (Mark 3:17). He is the only one of the Twelve whose death for the faith the New Testament records: King Herod (Herod Agrippa I) had him put to death with the sword (Acts 12:1–2).

people.name: John son of Zebedee
people.text: A fisherman called with his brother James (Mark 1:19–20), one of the three closest to Jesus. The Gospel of John speaks of “the disciple whom Jesus loved”, who leaned against Him at the supper, stood by the cross and testified to these things (John 13:23; John 19:26; John 21:20–24). It never names him; early church tradition identifies him with John and as the Gospel’s author.

people.name: Philip
people.text: From Bethsaida, the town of Andrew and Peter (John 1:44). He brought Nathanael to Jesus (John 1:45). At the last supper he asked, “Lord, show us the Father, and that will be enough for us” (John 14:8). Not to be confused with Philip the tetrarch, Herod’s son.

people.name: Nathanael
people.text: From Cana in Galilee (John 21:2). Brought by Philip, he first doubted that anything good could come from Nazareth, then said, “Rabbi, You are the Son of God!” (John 1:46–49). He does not appear in the lists of the Twelve; many identify him with Bartholomew, who is paired with Philip there.

people.name: Matthew (Levi)
people.text: A tax collector at Capernaum whom Jesus called from his tax booth. Mark and Luke call him Levi; the Gospel of Matthew calls him Matthew (Mark 2:14; Matthew 9:9). Early church tradition names him as the author of that Gospel.

people.name: Thomas
people.text: Called Didymus, “the twin”. When Jesus went back toward Judea, Thomas said, “Let us also go, so that we may die with Him” (John 11:16). Absent when the risen Jesus first came, he would not believe until he saw; a week later he said, “My Lord and my God!” (John 20:24–28).

people.name: Judas Iscariot
people.text: One of the Twelve. He kept the money bag and stole from it (John 12:6). He agreed with the chief priests to hand Jesus over for thirty pieces of silver (Matthew 26:14–15) and led the arresting crowd to Gethsemane. Filled with remorse, he returned the silver and died (Matthew 27:3–5; Acts 1:18).

people.name: Mary Magdalene
people.role: Witness of the empty tomb and the risen Jesus
people.text: Probably from Magdala on the lake. Jesus had driven seven demons out of her, and she was one of the women who supported Him “out of their own means” (Luke 8:2–3). She watched the crucifixion and the burial (Mark 15:40–47), and John tells how the risen Jesus appeared to her at the tomb (John 20:11–18). The idea that she had been a prostitute is a later Western tradition, not something the Gospels say.

people.name: Martha
people.text: Sister of Mary and Lazarus at Bethany, and a friend Jesus loved (John 11:5). Once she was busy with serving while Mary sat listening (Luke 10:38–42). When Lazarus died she told Jesus, “I believe that You are the Christ, the Son of God” (John 11:27).

people.name: Mary of Bethany
people.text: Sister of Martha and Lazarus. She sat at Jesus’ feet listening to His message (Luke 10:39), and six days before the Passover she anointed His feet with costly perfume (John 12:3).

people.name: Lazarus
people.text: Brother of Martha and Mary at Bethany. Jesus raised him after four days in the tomb (John 11:17–44). Because many believed in Jesus on his account, the chief priests planned to kill him as well (John 12:10–11).

people.name: Nicodemus
people.role: A Pharisee who came by night
people.text: A Pharisee and “a leader of the Jews” who came to Jesus at night (John 3:1–2). Later he urged the council to give Jesus a fair hearing (John 7:50–51), and he brought about seventy-five pounds of myrrh and aloes for Jesus’ burial (John 19:39).

people.name: Joseph of Arimathea
people.text: A rich man and a respected member of the council, “waiting for the kingdom of God” (Matthew 27:57; Mark 15:43), and a disciple of Jesus, though secretly (John 19:38). He asked Pilate for the body and laid it in his own new tomb (Matthew 27:60).

people.name: Simeon and Anna
people.text: Simeon, “righteous and devout”, had been promised that he would not die before seeing the Lord’s Christ; he took the baby in his arms and praised God (Luke 2:25–32). Anna, an elderly widow and prophetess, never left the temple and spoke about the child to all who were waiting for redemption (Luke 2:36–38).

people.name: Zacchaeus
people.text: A rich chief tax collector, too short to see over the crowd, who climbed a sycamore tree. Jesus stayed at his house, and Zacchaeus gave half his possessions to the poor and promised to repay fourfold anyone he had cheated (Luke 19:1–10).

people.name: Simon of Cyrene
people.text: A man from Cyrene in North Africa, coming in from the country, whom the soldiers forced to carry Jesus’ cross. Mark names his sons, Alexander and Rufus, as if his readers knew them (Mark 15:21).

people.name: Caesar Augustus
people.text: The first Roman emperor. Luke says his decree for a registration of the empire brought Joseph and Mary to Bethlehem (Luke 2:1–5).

people.name: Tiberius
people.text: Emperor during Jesus’ ministry. Luke dates John’s preaching to “the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar” (Luke 3:1). The “Caesar” of the coin question is probably Tiberius (Mark 12:16–17).

people.name: Herod the Great
people.text: King over the Jews under Rome, a great builder who rebuilt the temple on a grand scale. Matthew says he tried to kill the newborn king at Bethlehem (Matthew 2:16). He died at Jericho, usually dated 4 BC, and his kingdom was divided among his sons.

people.name: Archelaus
people.text: A son of Herod the Great who ruled Judea after him. Because of him, Joseph took the family to Galilee instead (Matthew 2:22). Rome removed him in AD 6 and sent a Roman governor to rule Judea.

people.name: Herod Antipas
people.role: Ruler of Galilee and Perea, 4 BC–AD 39
people.text: A son of Herod the Great and the “Herod” of Jesus’ ministry. He married Herodias, his brother’s wife, imprisoned John the Baptist for condemning it, and later had him beheaded (Mark 6:17–28). Jesus called him “that fox” (Luke 13:32). Pilate sent Jesus to him during the trials (Luke 23:7–12). Rome exiled him in AD 39.

people.name: Philip the tetrarch
people.text: A son of Herod the Great who ruled the lands north-east of the lake (Luke 3:1). He rebuilt Paneas as Caesarea Philippi and, according to Josephus, Bethsaida as Julias. Not to be confused with Philip the apostle.

people.name: Pontius Pilate
people.text: The Roman prefect who governed Judea. He found no basis for a charge against Jesus, yet handed Him over to be crucified (Luke 23:4; Mark 15:15). Luke mentions Galileans “whose blood Pilate had mixed with their sacrifices” (Luke 13:1). A stone inscribed with his name was found at Caesarea in 1961.

people.name: Caiaphas
people.text: High priest during Jesus’ ministry and son-in-law of Annas (John 18:13). He told the council “it is better for you that one man die for the people than that the whole nation perish” (John 11:50). Jesus was tried at his house before the council (Matthew 26:57).

people.name: Annas
people.text: High priest from AD 6 to 15 and still powerful afterward; five of his sons held the office, according to Josephus. Jesus was taken to him first on the night of the arrest (John 18:13).

words.text: Aramaic for “father”. Jesus prays “Abba, Father” in Gethsemane (Mark 14:36), and Paul says believers cry out the same words by the Spirit (Romans 8:15).
A Roman army officer in charge of about a hundred soldiers.

Messiah (Hebrew) and Christ (Greek) both mean “anointed one” (John 1:41). Israel’s kings were anointed with oil, and God had promised David a descendant whose throne He would establish forever (2 Samuel 7:12–16).

The highest Jewish court in Jerusalem, led by the high priest, with chief priests, elders and scribes (Mark 14:55; Mark 15:1). John records the leaders telling Pilate, “We are not permitted to execute anyone” (John 18:31); how far that applied is debated.
“Ten Cities”: a group of Greek-speaking cities, mostly east of the Jordan and the lake, where many Gentiles lived.
Hanukkah, in winter. It remembers how the temple was cleansed and rededicated in 164 BC after a Greek king defiled it (John 10:22).
A disciple is a student who follows a teacher and learns his way of life. An apostle is “one who is sent”: Jesus gave that name to the Twelve (Luke 6:13).
Anyone who is not Jewish. Gentiles could worship only in the temple’s outer court.
Aramaic for “the Place of the Skull” (Mark 15:22). The name Calvary comes from the Latin word for skull.
“Good news”: the message that God’s kingdom has come near in Jesus (Mark 1:15). The four books that tell His life are also called Gospels.

The high priest led the temple and the council. Under Rome he was appointed and removed by the governor or Herod’s family. The chief priests were senior priests from leading families, including former high priests.
From the Hebrew of Psalm 118:25, “save us, we pray”. By Jesus’ day it was also a shout of praise (Mark 11:9).
God’s rule as King, which Jesus announced had come near (Mark 1:15). Matthew usually says “kingdom of heaven”, with the same meaning (Matthew 4:17).
John the Baptist’s name for Jesus, “who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1:29). Many hear in it the Passover lamb and the sacrifices (compare Isaiah 53:7).
In the Bible, a range of skin diseases, not only the illness called leprosy today. Those who had it lived apart and had to cry out, “Unclean, unclean!” (Leviticus 13:45–46).
Learned men from the east, known for studying the stars and interpreting dreams (Matthew 2:1).
A short story or comparison from everyday life that teaches something about God and His kingdom.
The spring feast remembering Israel’s rescue from Egypt (Exodus 12). Lambs were sacrificed at the temple and eaten at a family meal in Jerusalem, followed by the seven days of Unleavened Bread.

Greek for “fiftieth”: the Feast of Weeks, a harvest feast about fifty days after Passover, counted from the offering of the first sheaf (Leviticus 23:15–16). On this day the Holy Spirit came (Acts 2).
A popular movement devoted to keeping the Law of Moses carefully, along with “the tradition of the elders” (Mark 7:3). They believed in the resurrection of the dead (Acts 23:8).
The Roman governor’s headquarters (Mark 15:16). Where Pilate’s stood in Jerusalem is debated.
“The day before the Sabbath” (Mark 15:42), when everything was made ready for the day of rest.
A respectful title meaning “teacher” (John 1:38; John 20:16).
To turn around: a change of mind and life, turning from sin back to God (Mark 1:15).
The seventh day, a day of rest from work (Exodus 20:8–11). It ran from sunset on Friday to sunset on Saturday. Many of Jesus’ disputes were about healing on it.
A party linked with the leading priestly families. They said there is no resurrection (Mark 12:18; Acts 23:8).
The people of Samaria, between Galilee and Judea. They kept the books of Moses but worshiped on Mount Gerizim, not in Jerusalem (John 4:20), and Jews and Samaritans avoided each other (John 4:9).
Experts in the Law of Moses who copied, studied and taught it (Mark 1:22).
The title Jesus used most for Himself. It recalls Daniel’s vision of “One like the Son of Man” given everlasting kingship (Daniel 7:13–14; Mark 14:62).
A town’s meeting place for prayer and for reading and teaching the Scriptures, especially on the Sabbath.
Also called the Feast of Booths: an autumn harvest feast when people lived in shelters for seven days, remembering the wilderness journey (Leviticus 23:42–43).
Local men who collected tolls and taxes for Herod’s family or for Rome, and often took more than was due (Luke 3:12–13). Many saw them as cheats and collaborators.
The temple in Jerusalem, the center of Jewish worship, where sacrifices were offered. Herod the Great rebuilt it on a grand scale, beginning about 20 BC; the Romans destroyed it in AD 70.
A ruler of part of a kingdom. Herod Antipas and Philip were tetrarchs (Luke 3:1).
The Gospels’ name for an evil spirit, also called a demon (Mark 1:23).
